findings.title: Identifying FortiGate Firmware From a Single ClientHello
findings.summary_md: VulnCheck published the underlying research behind this story, describing 375,904 internet-facing FortiGate hosts with the FGFM management port exposed in Target Intelligence data from 14 October to 12 November 2026. The post explains that each host answers a connection with a TLS ClientHello, which the team fingerprinted with JA4 to place hosts in six FortiOS generations and map them to CVE sets, including CVE-2024-23113 on port 541. It reports that 6.8 to 36.1 percent of the cohort is on end-of-support branches and provides Suricata and Snort rules for defenders.

findings.title: Identifying FortiGate Firmware From a Single ClientHello | Adam Powis
findings.summary_md: VulnCheck researcher Adam Powis published the findings on LinkedIn, stating that only 269 of 838,100 FortiOS hosts seen in Target Intelligence advertise a version. He said about 376,000 FortiGates leave a management port open and that 375,904 were placed into software version ranges. His post reports that 160,171 hosts, or 42.6 percent, are in generations where every version measured has a vulnerability known to be exploited in the wild.

findings.title: FortiGate TLS ClientHello Fingerprints Expose Firmware and CVE
findings.summary_md: SecOps Signal reported VulnCheck's research on 16 November 2026, describing roughly 375,904 exposed FGFM management ports on TCP 541 that leak firmware information through TLS handshakes. The article says the 30-day measurement ran from 14 October to 12 November 2026 and was queried on 13 November. It frames the risk as vulnerability mapping against internet-facing FortiGate devices and notes Fortinet's guidance that the port should not be public.

findings.title: Nearly 376,000 FortiGate hosts are exposing a management port to the internet
findings.summary_md: VulnCheck's company account amplified the same research on 19 November 2026, saying nearly 376,000 FortiGate hosts expose a management port that Fortinet says should stay private. The post describes Adam Powis's JA4 grouping of the hosts into six firmware generations and the use of those generations to identify potential exposure to known exploited vulnerabilities. It points readers to the full VulnCheck write-up.

findings.title: Format String Bug in fgfmd (FG-IR-24-029)
findings.summary_md: Fortinet's PSIRT advisory FG-IR-24-029, published 8 February 2024, describes CVE-2024-23113 as a use of an externally controlled format string in the FortiOS fgfmd daemon that allows unauthenticated remote code execution. It lists FortiOS 7.4.0 through 7.4.2, 7.2.0 through 7.2.6 and 7.0.0 through 7.0.13 as affected, with fixes in 7.4.3, 7.2.7 and 7.0.14. The advisory timeline records potential exploitation in the wild on 11 October 2024 and recommends removing fgfm access from interfaces as a workaround.

findings.title: Fortinet FortiGate CVE-2024-23113 - A Super Complex Vulnerability In A Super Secure Appliance In 2024
findings.summary_md: watchTowr published a technical analysis of CVE-2024-23113 on 14 October 2024, reverse engineering the format string flaw in FortiGate's fgfmd service and the FGFM protocol over TCP port 541. The post notes the vulnerability affected maintained FortiOS branches before patching and had been highlighted by CISA as exploited in the wild. It credits Fortinet's Gwendal Guégniaud with the discovery and describes reverse engineering the FGFM protocol to reproduce exploitation and build a detection artifact.
